title: Réaumur, Rømer, Newton: Legacy Temperature Scales in Old Manuals
h1: Réaumur, Rømer and Newton — legacy temperature scales you will still see
description: Antique European instruments and translated 18th-century texts still use Réaumur (0/80), Rømer (7.5/60) and Newton (0/33). Here are the exact conversions.

hero: Réaumur puts freezing water at 0 and boiling at 80. It still labels antique thermometers, brewing manuals and cheese ripening charts across Italy, Germany and Switzerland.
body: Three temperature scales survive in historical texts and antique instruments. Skipping the conversion misreads recipes and technical notes by tens of degrees Fahrenheit.

Réaumur: antique European thermometers, old cheesemaking and confectionery recipes, some brewery references. Rømer: Danish 18th-century instruments, occasionally in historical meteorology. Newton: historical physics texts before Fahrenheit and Celsius standardised.
20 °Ré × 5/4 = 25 °C = 77 °F. Skip the conversion and a room reader thinking 20 °Ré ≈ 20 °C would run the cave 5 °C too cold, slowing ripening by weeks and shifting the flavour profile.
Réaumur is the one you will hit most often. Convert by 5/4 to Celsius, then to whatever your instrument reads.

faqs.a: Yes. Réaumur, Rømer, Newton, Celsius, and Fahrenheit are all linear affine transforms of each other.
Effectively no — but it survives on antique glass thermometers and in restored recipes, especially Italian and Swiss cheese production notes.
